scope: Chronological changes through 1969 for OM-18, OM-28, OM-45, Small/Early, Classical. Editorial evidence only; remove source/dealer links from public article prose per Joe.

events.change: The first OM developed from the 000-28, adding a 14-fret neck/body joint while retaining the long scale.
events.scope: Model introduction, not a claim that every prototype shared the final production specifications.

events.change: Mahogany-bodied OM-18 production began with two guitars ordered January 15.
events.scope: Shop-order date, not shipping date.

events.change: The belly bridge replaced the early straight bridge forms: pyramid on early OM-28s; plain rectangular on the first OM-18s.
events.scope: Use year-level transition. Some unsold earlier guitars received belly bridges before leaving the factory.

events.change: Larger pickguards replaced the early small teardrop pattern.
events.scope: Firsthand Schoenberg example establishes larger guard with original banjo tuners by March 1931; do not claim simultaneous guard/tuner switch or exact common serial cutoff.

events.change: Conventional open-back guitar tuners replaced banjo-style tuners during the year.
events.scope: Corwin dates clipped-end G-98 guitar tuners to 1931-1934; his forum post cites Longworth log annotation on OM-18 stamped May 29, 1931. Year-level wording recommended. Full indexed forum text was retrieved through web search after direct open failed.

events.change: Style 18 fingerboard dots extended from frets 5, 7 and 9 to include frets 12 and 15.
events.scope: Style-wide published chronology. Do not treat later repair boards as production changes.

events.change: Style 28 diamonds-and-squares fingerboard decoration extended to the 12th and 15th frets.
events.scope: Earlier pattern occupied frets 5, 7 and 9.

events.change: The OM designation gave way to 000 while the early renamed guitars still retained the long scale.
events.scope: Keep factory designation. The name change and scale reduction were separate events.

events.change: The successor 000-18 and 000-28 changed from approximately 25.4 inches to 24.9 inches.
events.scope: Corwin gives September 12; manufacturer confirms only later in 1934. Use latter unless exact date is necessary.

events.change: Martin introduced T-shaped frets and steel T-bar neck reinforcement after the original OM run; original 1929-1933 OMs used bar frets and ebony reinforcement.
events.scope: Present as successor-era distinction. Do not suggest the original OM-45 adopted this system while still in regular production.

events.change: Eric Schoenberg ordered six OM-28s through the Folklore Center and Matty Umanov, reviving the model after its original run.
events.scope: Firsthand participant history. Do not infer that the 1969 guitars were exact copies of every prewar construction detail.

events.change: Martin introduced the pearl-trimmed OM-45 on the long-scale, 14-fret Orchestra Model platform.
events.scope: Original OM-45 production lasted through 1933.

events.change: The Deluxe added an inlaid pickguard and bridge, plus engraved gold tuners with pearl buttons. The solid headstock carried a simpler torch than earlier Style 45 heads.
events.scope: A separate trim variant, not a chronological replacement for the standard OM-45.

events.date: Within A Year Of Its 1930 Introduction
events.change: The Deluxe was discontinued while the standard OM-45 continued.
events.scope: Do not turn this into an exact 1931 cutoff. Corwin lists the last batch in November 1930, with later requests refused.

events.change: The original OM-45 run ended after 40 guitars built from 1930 through 1933.
events.scope: Manufacturer count does not resolve whether Deluxe is included; do not add a separate Deluxe total to 40.

events.change: Martin moved away from Stauffer-style one-sided tuners and adjustable-neck construction toward Spanish-influenced guitars and the later standardized styles.
events.scope: An era of overlapping designs; no single serial or date marks every feature transition.

events.change: Style numbers became associated with repeatable trim combinations; Style 28 used herringbone and Style 26 a half-herringbone border.
events.scope: Early custom combinations still existed. Do not label every earlier guitar by a later catalog style.

events.change: Size 0 expanded the concert range in the 1850s; size 00 followed in the 1870s; the larger 000 appeared in 1902.
events.scope: Avoid precise 0/00 introduction years: Corwin says 1854/1873, GuitarHQ 1852/1877. The 1902 000 date agrees with the factory history.

events.change: Martin began supplying koa Hawaiian guitars to Southern California Music Company, introducing a steel-string branch before its general Spanish-playing steel-string line.
events.scope: July 1916 shipments of six samples each are documented; the factory-history summary instead says 1917. Do not present all 1916 Martins as steel-string guitars.

events.change: Style 18 changed from rosewood to mahogany back and sides, retaining a spruce top.
events.scope: Style-wide change, excluding explicit special orders.

events.change: Style 28 body binding changed from elephant ivory to grained celluloid.
events.scope: Body binding only; not a claim that all ivory components ended together.

events.change: The all-mahogany 2-17 revived Style 17 as a lower-priced steel-string guitar.
events.scope: First standard Spanish-playing production steel-string Martins, not first Martin steel-string instruments of any kind.

events.change: Steel strings became standard on Style 18 Spanish-playing models.
events.scope: Gut-regulated guitars remained available by special order.

events.change: Style 28 joined the standard steel-string range.
events.scope: Not permission to fit current heavy strings to every surviving instrument.

events.change: Plain-wing rectangular bridges replaced pyramid bridges on Style 18.
events.scope: Separate from the later belly-bridge introduction.

events.change: Style 21 changed from pyramid to plain rectangular bridges.
events.scope: Not a statement about Style 28.

events.change: The 0-17 and 0-18 adopted 14-fret bodies as the '32 Model' versions.
events.scope: Limited to these named models; do not say every small Martin became 14-fret.

events.change: Style 18 rosewood body binding gave way to black Fiberloid.
events.scope: Followed by tortoise-colored plastic later in the 1930s, with smaller sizes changing earlier than dreadnoughts.

events.change: Most smaller Style 18 guitars briefly used rosewood fingerboards and bridges, before returning chiefly to ebony.
events.scope: Do not project D-18's later 1947 transition onto 0/00/000 models.

events.change: Smaller Style 18 models changed again to rosewood fingerboards and bridges.
events.scope: The source describes most production, not an exception-free serial cutoff.

events.change: The 0-16NY and 00-21NY brought back 12-fret, slotted-headstock designs with plain fingerboards, no pickguards and restrained finishes.
events.scope: 0-16NY is mahogany, 00-21NY rosewood. New Yorker models remained X-braced; do not classify them as the fan-braced G/C classical range.

events.change: Martin changed its usual steel-string bridge saddle from the long through-cut form to a short drop-in saddle.
events.scope: Apply to the relevant steel-string bridges, not every classical/tie bridge or historical special order.

events.change: Black Boltaron replaced tortoise-colored binding on Style 18.
events.scope: Corwin cites serial 212100. Year-level wording is adequate.

events.change: The G series restored a dedicated gut-string line after Martin's 1920s move toward steel strings.
events.scope: Early G experiments varied; do not claim all 1936 guitars already had the familiar later body/bracing configuration.

events.change: The familiar G construction paired a 12-fret neck with the outline of a 14-fret 00 body, fan bracing and a tie bridge.
events.scope: Describe as the established later configuration; no verified exact year for standardization. 00-18G was mahogany, 00-28G rosewood.

events.change: The C series succeeded the G line. The 00-18C used the traditional elongated 12-fret 00 outline with fan bracing; the rosewood 000-28C introduced the larger 000 body.
events.scope: Corwin dates 000-28C 1962-1969. RetroFret identifies 1965 as 00-18C's fourth production year.

events.change: The rosewood 00-28C joined the range as the smaller alternative to the 000-28C.
events.scope: Do not say the 000-28C disappeared immediately; its recorded run extends through 1969.

events.change: The mahogany N-10 and rosewood N-20 introduced a more Spanish-style classical body design.
events.scope: The previous draft omitted this because a dealer said 1969. Corwin and Gruhn both support 1968; Gruhn records twelve N-20s that year.

events.change: The early N-20 used a 25.4-inch scale and traditional Martin slotted headstock, with seven fan braces and no bridge plate.
events.scope: Keep the nominal early scale separate from the later 26.375-inch redesign, which is outside the through-1969 scope.

conflicts: OM bridge month: Corwin OM page says March 1930; specialist discussion places the change in early April. Use 1930.
OM tuner/guard changes should not be conflated. A March 1931 larger-guard OM-28 still has original banjo tuners.
Corwin OM page's caption for serial 54864 says December 1930 although narrative and serial establish December 1933. Do not copy the caption error.
OM-18 first two straight bridges are described partly as Corwin's reasoned reconstruction; phrase the 1930 bridge transition without claiming an inspected surviving first example.
OM-45 Deluxe counts conflict among histories. Omit a Deluxe production total. Five known is an undated researcher inventory, not an assured 2026 surviving census.
Corwin Deluxe page says impractical guard prompted discontinuation; OM page mentions difficulty sourcing distinctive parts. Avoid assigning a sole causal explanation.
Size 0 and 00 exact introduction years differ between established references. Use decades or resolve with factory archives.
Early X-bracing dates differ: older factory PDF says 1850s; photographed Corwin examples indicate 1840s. Use mid-19th-century development unless researching precise invention history separately.
0-15 introduction: one Corwin paragraph says added 1940 while another says introduction1939. Omit exactyear until resolved.
Do not extend steel-string neck rods, bridgeplate changes, or saddle transitions automatically to the G/C/N classical models.
Do not use a specimen repair, replacement tuner, altered neck, conversion, or modern reproduction specification as a model-wide factory change.
